analysis.one_liner: Requires private health insurance to cover medically necessary reconstructive care for children born with craniofacial birth defects.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2022, sent to three House committees, and never received a hearing or a vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required private health plans and insurers to cover diagnosis and treatment of congenital craniofacial, oral, and facial birth defects — conditions like cleft palates and facial differences present from birth. Coverage would have to include any medically necessary care to restore normal function or appearance, including dental, orthodontic, and prosthetic support, and insurers could not impose stricter limits or higher cost-sharing on this care than on other medical benefits. It was referred to three House committees and died there without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Children born with craniofacial anomalies and birth defects — such as cleft lip and palate and other facial or oral congenital conditions — and their families. The bill would require insurers to pay for medically necessary reconstructive surgery and related dental, orthodontic, and prosthetic care, and it would stop insurers from imposing tighter limits or higher cost-sharing on this care than on other medical benefits. Families who today often pay out of pocket for procedures insurers classify as cosmetic would see those costs covered from birth through completion of treatment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children with craniofacial birth defects and their families

how_it_helps.text: Requires group health plans and health insurers to cover diagnosis and treatment of craniofacial, oral, or maxillofacial congenital anomalies and birth defects.

Coverage must include any medically necessary service to functionally improve, repair, or restore a body part, including reconstructive surgery, dental, orthodontic, and prosthodontic support from birth through completion of treatment, as determined by the treating physician.

Bars insurers from applying coverage limits or cost-sharing to this care that are more restrictive than what the plan applies to other medical and surgical benefits, so families would not face extra hurdles for reconstructive care.
Requires plans to notify enrollees each year, in plain language, about these coverage rights.

analysis.who_pays: Private health insurers and self-insured employers, who would bear the cost of the newly required coverage; some of that cost would likely be passed into premiums and employee benefits. Families of affected children would gain far more than they pay, since their cost-sharing could be no more restrictive than for other medical benefits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employer health plans

drawbacks.text: The mandate would raise claim costs for private insurers and self-insured employers, and some of that cost would likely flow into premiums paid by all enrollees and benefits costs borne by employers.

The mandate reaches self-insured employer plans through ERISA and the tax code, adding a federal requirement to plans that employers currently design themselves; employers could adjust other benefits or cost-sharing to manage the added expense.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is large and concrete for a small, vulnerable group: children born with craniofacial anomalies would get medically necessary reconstructive care covered on the same terms as other surgery, instead of having it written off as cosmetic. The main cost is that insurance premiums and employer plans would absorb the added coverage, spreading it across all enrollees — though the bill caps cost-sharing at what plans already apply to other benefits, and prior versions of this concept have historically drawn broad bipartisan support. No serious design flaw appears on the face of the bill; the strongest objection is simply the mandate's cost to plans and the premium pressure it creates.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced, none of them acted on it, and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Neal Dunn introduced the bill on May 10, 2022, with one cosponsor, Rep. Morgan Griffith.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, and Ways and Means Committees the same day, and the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee received it.
No committee held a hearing, marked up the bill, or reported it out; the House never voted on it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
The bill was carried over from the 117th Congress and received no further action, which is the standard fate for bills that stall in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and self-insured employers are better off because no coverage mandate was enacted; families of children with craniofacial birth defects continue to fight plan denials on their own.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and employers avoiding a coverage mandate

for.name: Rep. Neal Dunn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House on May 10, 2022.

for.name: Rep. H. Morgan Griffith
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, the only cosponsor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, and Ways and Means Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor report — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Republican with a Republican cosponsor, but so few members acted on it that no partisan pattern in support or opposition can be read from the record; it simply never advanced out of committee.

industries.note: The bill would require private plans to cover reconstructive care for congenital craniofacial defects on terms no worse than other benefits, adding a mandated benefit they currently can deny or limit. The cost would largely be absorbed in premiums and plan design.

industries.industry: Reconstructive surgeons, hospitals, and dental/orthodontic providers
industries.note: Providers of craniofacial reconstructive care, including the dental and orthodontic specialists the bill explicitly covers, would see more of their services reimbursed by insurance rather than paid out of pocket by families.
Employer plans regulated through ERISA would have to add this coverage, raising benefits costs for large employers that fund their own plans.
